doom.driver: Iran live updates: Houthis claim new missile attack on Riyadh airport. President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
doom.blurb: DELAYS EXPECTED AT THE SAUDI TERMINALS
doom.summary: Eight months into America's war with Iran, the Houthis are aiming missiles at Riyadh's airport. The Dakar Rally has quietly packed up and left for somewhere with fewer interceptors overhead. Oil dropped 2% because traders now worry more about demand than about burning refineries, and Israel is running its biggest drill in years while analysts mutter about 1973. Brazil and Serbia handed democracy a rare good night, though Flávio Bolsonaro won't concede and the U.S. Justice Department is already suing over an Alaska Senate result that hasn't happened yet.

factors.name: AI Capability
factors.detail: SpaceX borrowed $40 billion for GPUs and Cerebras is serving trillion-parameter models, so the compute race keeps compounding.

factors.name: Governance
factors.detail: The DOJ wants to block Alaska's Senate results if the Republican loses, Bolsonaro refuses to concede, and Meta reportedly ignores a Brazilian court order.

factors.name: Geopolitics
factors.detail: The U.S.-Iran war grinds on, with Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites, Israel mobilizing divisions, and Ukraine still under fire.

factors.name: Alignment
factors.detail: No new safety incident today, just AI agents cold-pitching editors and an AI radio host winning over listeners.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Uganda imposed a 21-day quarantine on arrivals from DR Congo, U.S. measles cases have doubled, and protests across France keep turning violent.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. Silhouette composition at the departures hall of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, shortly after sunrise. The camera stands inside the terminal and looks out through a vast floor-to-ceiling glass curtain wall. Beyond the glass, a blood-orange sky burns above a flat gravel desert plateau, with a dust-choked horizon the color of molten rust. Heat shimmer rises off the apron. A single faint white contrail curves high in the sky, far off and ambiguous. On the far southern horizon, the hazy black silhouettes of Kingdom Centre with its arched opening and the tapered Al Faisaliyah tower stand against the glow. The airport's faceted diamond-roofed mosque is a jagged black shape at the edge of the apron, and the slender control tower rises against the sun. Parked Saudia jets, tails lit with a thin ember rim of light, sit dark and still on the apron, with no ground crews and no fuel trucks. Inside the hall, deep black volcanic underlighting rises from the floor and throws long shadows across polished travertine. In the foreground, two whole figures are silhouetted against the glass. One is a middle-aged man in a thobe and ghutra, standing rigid with a rolling suitcase beside him, his head tilted up toward the sky. Beside him, a small girl in an abaya clutches a stuffed toy and leans against his side. A dead departures board hangs above them, a blank black slab with no readable characters. Behind them, rows of empty seats and one abandoned luggage cart trail off into the dark. The palette is only blood orange, ember red, and deep black. Cool tones are almost entirely extinguished, and the figures are pure black cutouts with crisp stepped pixel edges.

minor: On the right, the parked jet seems to have two tail fins, one mid-fuselage and one at the far end. This is probably a second plane behind it overlapping, but it reads slightly oddly.
The girl blends into the man's silhouette, so the two figures read as one dark mass. Her outstretched hand is still clearly attached to her.
The luggage cart on the right is a hard-to-read dark shape and looks a bit like a chair. The floor reflections of the figures and suitcase are murky but acceptable.
The blank departures board is a plain black slab with no text, as intended.

dawn.driver: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
dawn.summary: Two years after they first marched for clean government, Serbia's students have won at the ballot box, and Aleksandar Vučić has conceded that his party lost a vote billed as a referendum on the country's future. Streets filled with celebrating crowds as a youth-led movement turned persistence into a peaceful change of power. Elsewhere, a simple liquid painted onto children's teeth in seconds was confirmed to stop cavities without drills or needles, and astronomers may have spotted the first moon ever found beyond our Solar System.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: Astronomers found evidence of the first moon outside our Solar System, and physicists held an antimatter particle for months to study how it differs from ordinary matter.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: Gabon has restored public access to social media, reconnecting millions of people with friends, family and news online.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: Serbia's student movement carried its campaign for honest government all the way to an election victory, and the country celebrated in the streets.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: A calm day for environmental headlines.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: At a College of Magic, kids from marginalized communities learn card tricks and candy conjuring, and come away with real confidence and creativity.

copy_pick.why: "SWEEP THE POLLS" gives the strongest single front-page verb, and the summary is the most specific because it names Vučić and his concession, while avoiding Candidate 2's stock "reminder" filler and Candidate 3's echoes of recent cards ("had a lively day too", "showing up").

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. NIGHT SCENE on a quiet Belgrade side street just after midnight, seen from across the cobbles. Deep blue-black shadows dominate the frame, and every light is artificial: warm golden-yellow streetlamps on curved iron posts and the glowing window of a small newsstand kiosk. The wide brick wall of a socialist-era apartment block fills the background, its layered, peeling protest posters and stencil graffiti lit in golden pools. The largest stencil is a glowing open doorway spilling golden light, with a fresh green sapling sprouting from its threshold. Beside it are hand-painted red handprints and a stylized student backpack. A lit linden tree leans into the lamplight, its leaves a vivid fresh green against the darkness. At the kiosk, newspapers are fanned across the counter, each front page showing a wordless pixel photo of fireworks blooming over a packed square, so the celebration appears only as printed news. A row of sixteen small candles in glass jars glows quietly along the curb beneath the wall, a respectful echo of the tragedy behind the movement. Faint tricolor bunting in red, blue, and white droops between two lampposts. Wet cobbles reflect the gold light and the green leaves. Far down the street, a thin band of pale gold dawn glows between the buildings. No people appear in the scene. Confident, steady warmth, with a clear golden-yellow and fresh green palette.

minor: The posters on the upper right wall show tiny glyph-like marks that stand in for writing. They are too small to read as gibberish.
The kiosk awning and roof merge into the brick wall at the right edge, so the shop's shape is a bit hard to read.
The red handprints on the wall are stencil graffiti, as intended, and read as painted marks rather than detached hands.
The sapling stands in front of the glowing doorway rather than growing out of its threshold, which looks slightly odd but still reads fine.
The candle row along the curb is roughly sixteen jars, and a few at the right end blur together.
